short: The tendency to stick with the current situation or default choice, even when switching to a better option would be easy.
kid: You always pick the same red crayon because it is the one you used yesterday. Even when a shiny blue one is right there, you keep the red.
detail: Status quo bias is the preference for keeping things as they are, so the current state or the default option is chosen more often than its merits justify. William Samuelson and Richard Zeckhauser documented it in 1988, and it is linked to loss aversion, regret aversion and the effort that deciding takes. In investing it shows up as holding an inherited portfolio unchanged, never rebalancing, leaving money in a low-interest savings account, or staying in a costlier regular mutual fund plan instead of the direct plan. Policymakers use it deliberately: making a good choice the default, such as automatic enrolment in a pension scheme, raises participation sharply. A common confusion is treating every decision to stay put as bias. Holding steady after a fresh review is rational; the bias is staying put without that review.
example: Say you hold ₹10 lakh in the regular plan of a mutual fund with an expense ratio of 1.5%, while the direct plan of the same fund charges 0.5%. By never switching, you pay about ₹10,000 a year more in costs (1% of ₹10 lakh), ignoring any tax or exit load on the switch.

short: Avoiding decisions, or making overly safe ones, because you fear the painful feeling of regret if the choice turns out badly.
kid: You don't swap your toy car for your friend's ball, because you worry you will miss the car and feel sad. So you keep it, even if the ball might be more fun.
detail: Regret aversion is the tendency to make choices that minimise the chance of later regret rather than those with the best expected outcome. It grows out of regret theory, developed in 1982 by Graham Loomes and Robert Sugden and, separately, by David Bell, and it explains several investor habits. People hold losing stocks too long because selling would make the mistake final, part of the disposition effect. They avoid buying after a fall in case it falls further, stay in cash after missing a rally, or follow the crowd so that if things go wrong they are not wrong alone. Errors of commission, acting and being wrong, usually feel worse than errors of omission, failing to act. The common confusion is with loss aversion: loss aversion is the pain of losing money, regret aversion the pain of having chosen wrongly.
example: Say you bought 500 shares of ABC Ltd at ₹200, investing ₹1,00,000, and the price falls to ₹140. Your holding is now worth ₹70,000, but you refuse to sell and move into a better stock because selling would lock in a ₹30,000 loss and confirm the mistake.

short: The habit of crediting your successes to your own skill while blaming your failures on bad luck or other people.
kid: When your block tower stands tall, you say you are a great builder. When it falls, you say the table wobbled, even if your wobbly block was the reason.
detail: Self-attribution bias, often called self-serving bias, is the tendency to attribute good outcomes to personal ability and bad outcomes to outside forces. For an investor, a winning trade confirms 'I am skilled', while a losing one is blamed on the market, the government or an operator. Because gains are counted as evidence and losses are explained away, the investor learns the wrong lessons and grows overconfident, which leads to heavier trading, larger bets and poor diversification. Studies of brokerage accounts, such as those by Brad Barber and Terrance Odean, find that the investors who trade most tend to earn the least after costs. A good defence is a trading journal that records the reasoning before each trade, so results can be judged honestly afterwards. Do not confuse it with confidence earned from a long, verified track record.
example: Say a trader makes three trades that gain ₹20,000 each and two that lose ₹45,000 each. They credit the ₹60,000 of gains to skill and blame the ₹90,000 of losses on bad luck, missing the fact that the net result is a ₹30,000 loss.

short: The tendency to value rewards now far more than slightly later ones, while being patient about choices that are all far in the future.
kid: One sweet right now feels better than two sweets tomorrow. But if both are a long time away, you happily wait one more day for two.
detail: Hyperbolic discounting describes how people discount future rewards at a rate that is steep for short delays and much gentler for long ones. Standard finance assumes exponential discounting, a constant rate per period, which keeps preferences consistent over time. Under hyperbolic discounting, preferences reverse: someone who today prefers ₹1,100 in 53 weeks to ₹1,000 in 52 weeks may, when week 52 arrives, grab the ₹1,000. Economists such as David Laibson modelled this as present bias. It helps explain undersaving for retirement, credit-card and buy-now-pay-later borrowing, and plans to start investing 'next month' that never happen. Remedies are commitment devices such as automatic SIP debits, lock-in products and default enrolment. A common confusion is treating all impatience as irrational; a high but constant discount rate is consistent. The problem is the gap between today's plan and tomorrow's action.
example: Offered ₹1,000 today or ₹1,100 in one week, many people take ₹1,000, giving up a 10% gain to avoid a seven-day wait. Offered ₹1,000 in 52 weeks or ₹1,100 in 53 weeks, the same people usually choose ₹1,100, even though the trade-off is identical: one extra week for ₹100 more.
formula: Hyperbolic: Present value = Amount / (1 + k x Delay); standard exponential: Present value = Amount / (1 + r)^t

short: Our tendency to explain events with neat cause-and-effect stories, even when chance or many hidden factors were really responsible.
kid: When your balloon pops, you might say the cat did it, because that is a nice story. But maybe it just bumped something sharp by chance.
detail: The narrative fallacy, a term popularised by Nassim Nicholas Taleb in The Black Swan (2007), is the urge to fit facts into a simple, satisfying story and then believe that the story explains, and can predict, what happened. In markets it appears in daily commentary that attaches a reason to every move, such as 'Sensex falls on global cues', even when the move is within normal day-to-day noise. Investors buy a stock because a founder's journey or a theme like electric vehicles makes a compelling tale, not because cash flows justify the price. Stories make us overconfident because they leave out randomness and the evidence that does not fit. A useful check is to ask what the numbers say, what the base rate is, and what would prove the story wrong. The confusion to avoid is thinking every story is false; the danger is believing one without testing it.
example: Say XYZ Ltd rises 8% on a day when headlines credit its new CEO. If XYZ usually moves in line with its sector and the sector index rose 7% that day, only about 1 percentage point of the move is specific to XYZ, so the CEO story explains very little of it.

short: The idea that people make decisions with limited information, time and brainpower, so they aim for good-enough choices rather than the perfect one.
kid: In a big toy shop you can't look at every toy before home time. So you pick the first one that is really fun and say, this one is good enough.
detail: Bounded rationality, introduced by Herbert Simon, who won the 1978 Nobel Prize in economics, holds that people are rational only within limits: they have incomplete information, finite time and a limited ability to process what they know. Rather than optimising across every possibility, they satisfice, searching until they find an option that clears an acceptable bar, and they rely on rules of thumb called heuristics. This explains why investors lean on shortcuts such as star ratings, past returns or a friend's tip, and why companies follow simple budgeting rules. Heuristics are often sensible, but they also produce the systematic biases that behavioural finance studies. The common confusion is to equate bounded rationality with irrationality: satisficing can be a sensible response to the cost of gathering and processing information. The idea challenges the textbook homo economicus, who knows everything and calculates perfectly.
example: Say an investor wants an equity fund but cannot compare all 40 options on a platform. She checks the first 5, sets a rule of a five-year average return above 12% and an expense ratio below 1%, and buys the first fund that clears both bars, a satisficing choice rather than a full search.

short: The textbook model of a person who is perfectly rational, fully informed and self-interested, always choosing what gives them the most benefit.
kid: Imagine a robot friend who always knows the very best toy to pick, and never gets tired or cross. Real people are not quite like that.
detail: Homo economicus, or 'economic man', is the idealised decision-maker assumed in much of classical economics and finance. This agent has stable, consistent preferences, uses all available information correctly, updates beliefs by the rules of probability, and chooses whatever maximises expected utility, usually in pursuit of self-interest. The assumption makes models manageable and underpins ideas such as rational expectations and the efficient market hypothesis. Behavioural economists, notably Daniel Kahneman, Amos Tversky and Richard Thaler, showed that real people deviate in predictable ways: they feel losses more than equal gains, procrastinate, and are swayed by how choices are framed. India's Economic Survey 2018-19 drew exactly this contrast in a chapter on nudges. The common confusion is that the model claims everyone behaves this way; it is a simplifying benchmark, most useful for spotting where actual behaviour departs from it.
example: In the ultimatum game, one player proposes how to split ₹100 and the other can accept or reject; if they reject, both get nothing. Homo economicus would accept even ₹1, because ₹1 beats ₹0, but in experiments many real people reject offers of ₹20 or less as unfair.
formula: Expected utility = Sum of (probability of each outcome x utility of that outcome)

short: A gentle change in how choices are presented that steers people toward better decisions without banning options or changing incentives much.
kid: If fruit is put at the front of the lunch table and sweets at the back, more children pick fruit. Nobody is stopped from having sweets; the fruit is just easier to reach.
detail: A nudge is any feature of choice architecture, the way options are designed and presented, that predictably changes behaviour without forbidding any option or significantly changing economic incentives. Richard Thaler and Cass Sunstein popularised the idea in their 2008 book Nudge, and Thaler's 2017 Nobel Prize in economics recognised his wider work in behavioural economics. Common tools are defaults, reminders, simpler forms, social comparisons and well-timed prompts. The best-known finance example is automatic enrolment in workplace retirement plans, which raises participation far more than education alone. Governments and regulators use nudges for savings, tax compliance and disclosures, and India's Economic Survey 2018-19 devoted a chapter to them; companies use them in app design. The common confusion is calling any persuasion a nudge: a ban, mandate or large tax is not one, and design that steers people against their own interest is often called sludge or a dark pattern.
example: Say ABC Ltd offers its 1,000 employees a retirement savings plan. When employees must sign up themselves, 400 join; when everyone is enrolled automatically with a simple opt-out, 900 stay in. Changing only the default adds 500 savers, lifting participation from 40% to 90%.

short: The belief that you can profit from buying an overpriced asset because someone else, a 'greater fool', will later pay even more for it.
kid: You give one coin for a plain pebble, not because you like it, but because you think a friend will give you two coins for it. If no friend wants it, you are stuck with a pebble.
detail: The greater fool theory says an asset's price can keep rising even when it is above any sensible estimate of its worth, because buyers are not paying for its income or cash flows but for the chance to sell it on to someone willing to pay more. The strategy works only while new buyers keep arriving with money and optimism. When they run out, there is no one left to sell to, and the last holders absorb the losses as prices fall back towards fundamental value. It is a driver of asset bubbles, seen in episodes from tulip mania to dot-com shares, meme stocks and speculative tokens. The common confusion is with ordinary investing: someone buying for dividends, earnings or rent has a fallback value if prices stop rising, while a greater-fool buyer has only the hope of a resale.
example: Say you buy a speculative token for ₹500 that produces no income, hoping to sell it at ₹800 for a ₹300 gain. If buyers vanish and the price collapses to ₹100, you lose ₹400 per token, or 80% of what you paid.

short: Keynes's term for the instincts, moods and confidence that drive people to invest, spend and take risks, beyond what cold calculation would justify.
kid: Some days you feel brave and want to try the big slide; other days you feel shy and stay on the swings. Grown-ups have brave days and shy days too, and it changes what they build and buy.
detail: Animal spirits is John Maynard Keynes's phrase, from The General Theory (1936), for the 'spontaneous urge to action rather than inaction' behind many investment decisions. Because the long-run returns on a new factory or business cannot be calculated precisely, Keynes argued that confidence, optimism and emotion fill the gap. When animal spirits are strong, firms invest, banks lend and households spend, which can lift the whole economy; when they fade, even cheap money may fail to revive activity. George Akerlof and Robert Shiller revived the idea in their 2009 book Animal Spirits, linking it to confidence, fairness, corruption, money illusion and the stories people tell. Economists track it through business and consumer confidence surveys, such as those the RBI publishes. The common confusion is to treat it as pure irrationality; Keynes saw it as a natural response to genuine uncertainty.
example: Say a business survey shows the share of firms expecting better conditions rise from 50% to 70%, and their planned capital spending jumps from ₹40,000 crore to ₹48,000 crore, a 20% increase, while interest rates and current orders have barely changed. That confidence-driven jump is animal spirits at work.

short: Investor enthusiasm that pushes asset prices well above what fundamentals such as company earnings can justify, often a sign of a bubble.
kid: Everyone at the party gets so excited about one sticker that they offer five sweets for it. It is still just a sticker, and soon they wish they had kept their sweets.
detail: Irrational exuberance is the phrase US Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan used in a speech on 5 December 1996, asking how policymakers would know when it had 'unduly escalated asset values'. Economist Robert Shiller made it the title of his 2000 book, which argued that US share prices were far above levels justified by earnings and dividends, shortly before the dot-com crash. It describes a self-reinforcing mood in which rising prices attract new buyers, media stories and easy credit, which push prices higher still. Shiller's cyclically adjusted price-to-earnings ratio, or CAPE, is one gauge used to judge whether valuations look stretched. The common confusion is to use the phrase for any strong rally; prices can rise sharply for good reasons. It applies when valuations have drifted far from fundamentals and the main support for prices is the expectation of further gains.
example: The US Nasdaq Composite index closed at a peak of 5,048.62 on 10 March 2000 and fell to 1,114.11 by 9 October 2002 as the dot-com bubble burst. That is a fall of about 78% in roughly two and a half years.

short: The overall mood of investors towards a market or asset, whether they are broadly optimistic and buying or fearful and selling.
kid: When all the children in the playground are happy, everyone wants to join the game. When a few look worried, the others get worried too and stop playing.
detail: Market sentiment is the prevailing attitude of investors, bullish when optimism dominates and bearish when fear does, as distinct from fundamentals such as earnings, interest rates and cash flows. Because prices are set by people, sentiment can move markets for days or months on its own, and it often overshoots. It is measured indirectly through volatility indices such as India VIX, the put-call ratio in options, flows from foreign and domestic investors, the advance-decline ratio, investor surveys and levels of margin borrowing. 'Risk-on' and 'risk-off' describe broad swings in sentiment across asset classes. Many investors treat extreme readings as contrarian signals, buying when gloom is widespread and trimming when euphoria is. The common confusion is to assume sentiment explains prices in the long run: over long horizons earnings and cash flows matter more, while sentiment mainly drives short-term swings.
example: Say on index options there is open interest of 15 lakh put contracts and 12 lakh call contracts. The put-call ratio is 15 / 12 = 1.25, meaning traders hold 25% more puts than calls, which many read as cautious sentiment.

short: The two emotions said to drive markets: greed pushes prices up as investors chase gains, fear pushes them down as investors rush to safety.
kid: When everyone wants the last cupcake, they grab fast and offer a lot. When someone says the cupcakes might be bad, everyone drops them at once.
detail: Fear and greed describes the emotional cycle behind many market moves. Greed, the urge to make more and not miss out, drives buying, borrowing and speculation in rallies; fear, the urge to avoid losses, drives panic selling and a rush into cash or government bonds in sell-offs. Warren Buffett's well-known advice is to be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful. The idea has been turned into gauges such as CNN Business's Fear & Greed Index, which combines seven indicators, including market momentum, put and call options activity, junk bond demand and volatility, into a score from 0 (extreme fear) to 100 (extreme greed). In India, the India VIX volatility index is often called the fear gauge. The common confusion is to treat such indices as precise timing tools; extreme readings can persist for weeks or months.
example: Say a simple sentiment gauge averages three indicators, each scored from 0 to 100, which read 20, 30 and 40 today. The overall score is (20 + 30 + 40) / 3 = 30, in the fear zone, where a contrarian might start buying slowly while a momentum trader might wait.

short: A period when the price of an asset, such as shares, property or a cryptocurrency, rises far above its underlying value and then often collapses.
kid: A soap bubble grows bigger and bigger and looks lovely, but it is mostly air. One little poke and pop, it is gone.
detail: An asset bubble forms when prices climb well beyond what fundamentals such as earnings, rents or cash flows can support, sustained mainly by the expectation of further price rises. Economist Hyman Minsky and historian Charles Kindleberger described a common pattern: a new opportunity or technology, a credit-fuelled boom, euphoria as ordinary investors pile in, insiders taking profits, and finally panic as prices crash. Famous examples include Dutch tulip mania in the 1630s, the South Sea Bubble of 1720, Japan's late-1980s share and land bubble, the dot-com bubble of 2000 and the US housing bubble before the 2008 crisis. India saw a speculative surge in 1992 linked to the Harshad Mehta securities scam. Bubbles matter because their collapse can damage banks and the wider economy. The common confusion: a bubble is hard to prove in real time, since high prices may reflect genuine growth.
example: Japan's Nikkei 225 index closed at a record 38,915.87 on 29 December 1989 after a speculative boom, then fell to 7,054.98 by March 2009, a drop of about 82%. It did not close above its 1989 peak until February 2024.

short: An investor who trades on rumours, tips, hype or random price moves, believing they are useful information when they are not.
kid: Imagine children rushing to one side of the playground because someone shouted, without checking if anything is there. They run because of noise, not because they know something.
detail: A noise trader buys and sells on signals that carry no real information about value, such as rumours, social-media tips, chart patterns with no proven edge, or simple price momentum, while believing they are trading on information. Fischer Black's 1986 paper 'Noise' argued that such trading is what keeps markets liquid, because informed traders need someone to trade with. In 1990, De Long, Shleifer, Summers and Waldmann showed that noise traders' shifting moods can push prices away from fundamental value, and that rational arbitrageurs may not correct this because the mispricing can grow before it shrinks. This noise-trader risk is a core reason for limits to arbitrage, and it helps explain bursts of volatility and meme-stock episodes. The common confusion is to equate noise traders with small retail investors; professionals can trade on noise too, and many retail investors trade on genuine research.
example: Say a stock's fair value is ₹100 and noise traders bid it up to ₹120 on a social-media rumour. An arbitrageur who sells it short at ₹120 expects a ₹20 gain per share, but if the hype pushes the price to ₹140 first, they face a ₹20 loss per share and may be forced to close out before the price returns to ₹100.

short: The costs and risks that stop well-informed traders from fully correcting mispriced assets, allowing prices to stay wrong for long periods.
kid: You see one shop selling sweets cheaper than another, but the walk is long, your bag is small and the price might change before you get there. So the difference stays.
detail: Limits to arbitrage is the idea, set out by Andrei Shleifer and Robert Vishny in 1997, that arbitrage in real markets is risky and costly, so prices can stay away from fundamental value for long periods. Textbook arbitrage is riskless, but real mispricing trades face fundamental risk, since news may move the asset against you; noise-trader risk, since the mispricing can widen before it closes; and implementation costs, such as borrowing fees for short selling, short-sale restrictions and margin calls. Arbitrageurs also often manage other people's money, and investors may withdraw capital after losses, forcing exits at the worst time, as happened to Long-Term Capital Management in 1998. Known anomalies include the twin shares of Royal Dutch and Shell trading at inconsistent prices, and 3Com in 2000 being worth less than its stake in Palm. Persistent mispricing does not mean easy money.
example: Say a fund believes ABC Ltd is worth ₹100 while it trades at ₹130, and borrows and sells short 10,000 shares. Hype then pushes the price to ₹160, creating a mark-to-market loss of ₹3 lakh (₹30 x 10,000). If the fund cannot meet its broker's margin call, it must buy back and book that ₹3 lakh loss, even if the price later drops to ₹100.

short: The idea that investors react too strongly to dramatic news, pushing prices too far, so that extreme winners and losers later partly reverse.
kid: When one child trips, everyone shouts that the whole game is ruined. A bit later they see it was only a small bump and start playing again.
detail: The overreaction hypothesis, tested by Werner De Bondt and Richard Thaler in 1985, proposes that investors give too much weight to recent, vivid news and too little to long-run averages, so prices overshoot. Their study of US stocks found that portfolios of the biggest losers over the previous three to five years went on to beat portfolios of the biggest winners over the following years, consistent with prices reverting after an overreaction. This long-term reversal underpins contrarian and value strategies. The opposite pattern, underreaction, shows up over shorter horizons: prices adjust only gradually to news such as earnings surprises, producing momentum and post-earnings-announcement drift. Both challenge the efficient market hypothesis, which says prices respond quickly and correctly to new information. The common confusion is to assume every sharp fall is an overreaction; sometimes the news is worse than the market first assumed.
example: Say bad news sends ABC Ltd from ₹200 to ₹120, a 40% fall, while a careful valuation suggests ₹150 is fair. If the price later recovers to ₹150, an investor who bought at ₹120 gains ₹30 per share, a 25% return, as the overreaction unwinds.

short: The tendency to hold on to an existing view and update it too slowly when new evidence arrives.
kid: You think your friend doesn't like peas. Then you watch them eat a big plate of peas, but you still say they don't like peas, or change your mind only a tiny bit.
detail: Conservatism bias is the tendency to underweight new information relative to existing beliefs, so views change too little and too late. Psychologist Ward Edwards documented it in 1968: people revised their estimates in the right direction but by much less than Bayes' rule, the correct way to combine prior beliefs with new evidence, required. In markets, analysts who are slow to revise earnings forecasts after a surprise, and investors anchored to their original thesis, help explain underreaction, momentum and post-earnings-announcement drift. It belongs to the family of belief-perseverance biases, alongside confirmation bias and cognitive dissonance. Remedies include writing down in advance what evidence would change your view and revisiting forecasts after every set of results. The common confusion is with prudence: a conservative investor who prefers lower risk is making a sensible choice, while conservatism bias is a failure to process information properly.
example: Say an analyst forecasts annual earnings per share of ₹50 for ABC Ltd, and a weak quarter suggests about ₹40 is now realistic. If she trims her forecast only to ₹48, she has moved just 20% of the way towards the evidence: ₹2 of a ₹10 gap.
formula: Bayes' rule: P(belief | evidence) = P(evidence | belief) x P(belief) / P(evidence); conservatism means updating by less than this implies

short: The mental discomfort of holding beliefs, or a belief and an action, that clash, which people often ease by ignoring or twisting facts.
kid: You told everyone your kite is the best, but it keeps falling down. That feels yucky inside, so you blame the wind instead of looking at the kite.
detail: Cognitive dissonance, a theory developed by psychologist Leon Festinger in 1957, is the discomfort of holding conflicting ideas, for example 'I am a smart investor' and 'my stock has halved'. People often reduce the discomfort not by changing their minds but by avoiding or dismissing contrary information, seeking reassurance from those who agree, or rationalising the original decision. For investors this leads to holding losers too long, ignoring warning signs in results or governance, adding to falling positions to prove the first call right, and refusing to read critical research. It reinforces confirmation bias and the disposition effect. Practical defences include setting exit rules before buying and asking a neutral person to review the investment case. The common confusion is to treat the discomfort itself as the problem; it is a useful signal that the evidence may have changed and deserves a fresh look.
example: Say you invest ₹2 lakh in XYZ Ltd after praising it to friends, and the shares fall 35%, leaving ₹1.3 lakh. Instead of reading the latest results, which show falling sales, you skip the news and tell yourself the market simply does not understand the company.

short: The belief that you can influence outcomes that are actually mostly or entirely down to chance.
kid: When you blow on the dice before rolling, you might feel you made the six come up. But the dice was just lucky; blowing on it didn't help.
detail: The illusion of control, identified by psychologist Ellen Langer in 1975, is the tendency to overestimate how much one's actions affect outcomes that are largely random. In one of her experiments, people who picked their own lottery ticket valued it more than people who were simply handed one. In investing it shows up as frequent trading, intraday and options speculation, faith in elaborate chart setups and concentrated bets, all driven by the feeling that more activity means more control. It feeds overconfidence and, together with trading costs, erodes returns. In India, SEBI's September 2024 study found that about 93% of individual traders in equity futures and options made losses over FY22 to FY24. The common confusion is to deny that skill exists; research, discipline and risk management do matter. The illusion lies in believing effort and familiarity can control what is fundamentally uncertain.
example: Say a trader places 40 trades a month and pays about ₹50 per trade in brokerage, exchange charges and taxes. That is ₹2,000 a month, or ₹24,000 a year, spent before making any profit, a cost that grows with the feeling that more activity means more control.

short: The tendency to favour spending or comfort today over long-term goals like saving and investing, because sticking to a plan is hard.
kid: You plan to save your coins in the piggy bank for a big toy. But every time you pass the sweet shop you spend a coin, so the piggy bank stays light.
detail: Self-control bias is the failure to act on long-term goals because discipline gives way when short-term temptations appear. It is closely linked to hyperbolic discounting: a plan made calmly for the future yields to the pleasure available now. In personal finance it shows up as undersaving for retirement, overspending on credit cards, dipping into emergency or retirement money, and abandoning an investment plan during a market fall. In portfolios it can also show up as an excessive preference for income today, such as chasing high-dividend stocks, over long-term growth. Writers such as Michael Pompian classify it as an emotional bias, which is hard to fix with information alone, so the usual remedies are structural: pay yourself first, automate investing through SIPs, use lock-in products and keep separate accounts for separate goals. The common confusion is to see it as a character flaw; almost everyone has it.
example: Say Rohan earns ₹60,000 a month and plans to invest ₹10,000 of it each month, but usually spends the money before the month ends. Over a year he misses ₹1,20,000 of planned investment; a SIP that debits ₹10,000 on payday removes the daily temptation.

short: The tendency to invest in products or companies that reflect who you are or what you value, rather than judging them on expected returns.
kid: You want the toy with your favourite cartoon on it, even if another toy is better and lasts longer. You pick it because it feels like you.
detail: Affinity bias in behavioural finance is the tendency to make investment choices based on how a product or company expresses one's identity, values or loyalties, rather than on its risk and return. Examples include buying shares of a favourite consumer brand, an employer, a local company or a firm linked to one's community, or picking an ethical fund for the good feeling without checking its holdings and costs. Values-based investing is perfectly reasonable when done knowingly; the bias is when the feeling replaces the analysis. The same pull makes people trust schemes promoted within their own religious, ethnic or professional group, which fraudsters exploit in what is called affinity fraud; Bernard Madoff's Ponzi scheme drew heavily on such networks. Affinity fraud is the scam, affinity bias the weakness it preys on. Outside finance, affinity bias also means favouring people similar to yourself, for example in hiring.
example: Say you have ₹5 lakh to invest and put ₹3 lakh into ABC Ltd because you love its products, leaving ₹2 lakh for everything else. That is 60% of your money in one company, so a 40% fall in its share price alone would cut your whole portfolio by 24%.

short: The tendency to let one good impression, such as a famous brand or charismatic leader, colour your judgement of everything else about it.
kid: If a new friend has a really cool hat, you might think they must be good at everything. But a cool hat doesn't mean they can sing or share well.
detail: The halo effect, first described by psychologist Edward Thorndike in 1920, is a bias in which one positive trait shapes how we judge other, unrelated traits. In investing it leads people to assume that a famous, admired or fast-growing company must also be a good investment at any price, or that a charismatic founder guarantees sound governance and accounting. It can make investors overlook stretched valuations, weak cash flows or related-party dealings, and it inflates demand for popular IPOs. Phil Rosenzweig's book The Halo Effect showed how business writers praise the same company's strategy and culture when results are good and criticise them once results decline. The reverse, the horns effect, unfairly marks down everything about a company after one bad event. The key confusion to avoid: a great company and a great stock are different things, because the price may already reflect the greatness.
example: Say ABC Ltd, an admired brand, earns ₹20 per share and trades at ₹1,600, a P/E of 80. If earnings grow a healthy 10% to ₹22 but investors cut the P/E to 50, the price falls to ₹1,100, a 31.25% loss despite a good business year.

short: George Soros's theory that investors' beliefs move prices, and those price moves then change the real business conditions the beliefs were about.
kid: If all your friends think a game is fun, more children come to play, and the game really does get more fun. If everyone thinks it is boring, they leave and it becomes boring.
detail: Reflexivity is investor George Soros's theory, set out in The Alchemy of Finance (1987), that market participants' views and market prices influence each other in a two-way feedback loop. Standard theory treats fundamentals as independent: prices simply reflect them. Soros argued that prices can also change the fundamentals. A rising share price lets a company raise equity or borrow cheaply, make acquisitions and report faster growth, which seems to justify the higher price; rising house prices increase the value of collateral, which expands lending and pushes prices up further. The loop runs in reverse in a bust, when falling prices tighten credit and damage the businesses themselves. Soros used it to explain boom-bust cycles that models of stable equilibrium miss. The common confusion is with simple momentum: reflexivity is about prices altering the underlying reality, not just prices following prices.
example: Say ABC Ltd wants to raise ₹500 crore by issuing new shares. At a share price of ₹200 it must issue 2.5 crore shares, but if the price halves to ₹100 it must issue 5 crore shares, twice as many new shares and much heavier dilution for existing owners, so the share price itself changes how cheaply the company can fund its growth.
